analysis.one_liner: Permanently repeals the federal estate tax on inherited wealth.
analysis.headline: The bill to permanently repeal the estate tax was referred to the Ways and Means Committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have eliminated the federal estate tax, the tax levied on large inheritances passed on after death, for everyone dying after December 31, 2016. Because the tax applies only to very large estates, repealing it would have cut taxes almost exclusively for the wealthiest families. The bill never got a hearing or a vote: after introduction, it went to the Ways and Means Committee and stayed there until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Families inheriting very large estates. The federal estate tax exempts the first several million dollars and applies only to the largest estates, so eliminating it would have saved heirs of large fortunes tens of millions of dollars or more in taxes, while also preserving 'stepped-up basis,' which erases capital gains taxes on appreciated assets inherited at death.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals chapter 11 of the Internal Revenue Code, the federal estate tax, for estates of decedents dying after December 31, 2016.

Retains stepped-up basis at death, which resets the taxable value of inherited assets to their value on the day of death, erasing capital gains taxes on the appreciation that accumulated during the decedent's lifetime.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, and by extension taxpayers generally, would have lost the revenue the estate tax raises from the largest estates, or that money would have had to be made up from other taxes or borrowing. No one but large estate heirs would have gained anything from the bill.

drawbacks.text: The estate tax applies only to very large estates, with generous exemptions well above the net worth of nearly all American families, so the benefit of repeal would flow almost entirely to the heirs of the wealthiest households.

The bill retains stepped-up basis, which means the appreciated value of inherited stocks, businesses, and property would escape income tax entirely as well — a compounding of tax advantages available only to inheritors of substantial assets.
Repealing the tax would eliminate federal revenue, requiring either offsetting tax increases, spending cuts, or larger deficits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains go to a small number of very wealthy heirs; the costs — lost revenue and a larger permanent shield on inherited wealth — fall on everyone else. For an ordinary family, whose estate would fall far below the exemption threshold, the bill offers nothing.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Representative Robert Latta of Ohio introduced the bill on January 11, 2017, joined by eight Republican cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on the day of introduction; the action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and the bill died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Heirs to large estates remain subject to the estate tax as it stood, so wealthy families gained nothing from the bill's failure — but they lost nothing either. The broader public was spared the revenue loss and the expanded tax shield on inherited wealth that repeal would have created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the bill simply died quietly

for.name: Rep. Robert E. Latta
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to permanently repeal the estate tax on January 11, 2017.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never held a hearing, markup, or vote, letting it die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All ten sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, with no Democratic support recorded; the bill never advanced far enough for a roll-call vote.

industries.note: Repeal would have spared heirs of very large estates the estate tax and, with stepped-up basis retained, also the capital gains tax on inherited appreciation. The bill died, so this group keeps paying as before.
Law firms and advisors who manage estate-tax planning would lose a major line of business if the tax disappeared; the bill's failure preserves that business.

Proponents of estate tax repeal often cite heirs facing tax on inherited farms or closely held businesses; repeal would have removed that exposure, though these estates already benefit from exemptions and special valuation rules.
